context.hint: A Go session service has a verified one-hunk parser repair that rejects disabled account tokens after a pristine-tree patch application and preserves enabled, project-role, revoked-identifier, and password-time controls. The remaining boundary is the server authentication middleware: when a validly signed disabled-account token is presented, does it return the parser's unauthenticated error, or does it silently create an anonymous request? A valid enabled token must still put its subject into the handler context.
context.surface: A Go authorization service with a session manager, an account and project settings store, a token parser with separate account and project-role branches, server authentication middleware, and package-level tests backed by fake settings clients.
assumptions: The observer can read and modify a disposable local source tree, run the local Go toolchain, and create fake settings clients; no public target, production service, or installed dependency is used.
The attacker holds an existing validly signed token for an account that is later disabled and cannot change the server signing key.
An enabled account token and a project-role token are legitimate controls that must keep working.
Stored token-identifier removal and password modification time are existing revocation mechanisms that must keep working after the repair.
Official benchmark evaluation is host-side; local package tests and a clean patch application are not an official pass.

incumbent.text: Hypothesis: the saved one-hunk patch applies to a pristine source copy and reproduces disabled-account rejection there. Prerequisites: the pristine source snapshot, the saved patch, a local Go toolchain, and the test harness copied separately from the development tree. Bounded test: copy the snapshot fresh, run a patch dry check, apply only the hunk, copy the harness without other source edits, and replay a disabled valid-identifier token plus an enabled control. Expected supporting result: the hunk applies, the disabled token is rejected, and the enabled token is accepted. Falsifier: the hunk rejects or fuzzes context, the disabled token is accepted, or any extra source edit is required. Cleanup: remove the temporary tree.

candidates.text: Hypothesis: the authentication middleware distinguishes a parser rejection from an absent token and returns an unauthenticated error for the disabled account. Prerequisites: a local server fixture built on the pristine patched source, a valid disabled-account token, and an enabled control token. Bounded test: present both tokens through the middleware token slot, inspect the returned status and handler-context subject, and compare with an absent-token request. Expected supporting result: the disabled token yields an unauthenticated disabled error, the enabled token yields its subject, and only the absent token follows anonymous fallback. Falsifier: the disabled token yields a successful anonymous context. Cleanup: close the fixture and discard temporary clients.

Hypothesis: an enabled account token still propagates its specific subject into the handler context after the repair, so the middleware does not over-block legitimate sessions. Prerequisites: a patched local server fixture and an enabled account with a valid identifier. Bounded test: present the enabled token through the middleware and inspect the context subject; compare with an absent-token request. Expected supporting result: no error and the exact enabled subject. Falsifier: a missing or anonymous subject, or an unexpected rejection. Cleanup: reset the fixture.

Hypothesis: project-role tokens remain independent of account enabled state at the middleware boundary because their parser branch runs before account handling. Prerequisites: a patched server fixture, a project role with a stored role identifier, and an account flag that can be disabled. Bounded test: send a project-role token after disabling an associated account and inspect status and subject; compare with an enabled-account token. Expected supporting result: the role token is accepted with its role subject. Falsifier: the middleware rejects it with an account-state error. Cleanup: reset the project and account fixtures. Limitation: the server fixture may need a started project informer, so this is secondary to the account-token boundary.

Hypothesis: concurrent enable and disable toggles do not create intermittent middleware acceptance because the parser reads a copied account view. Prerequisites: a mutable fake settings store and a valid token. Bounded test: toggle the account flag in a loop while presenting the same token to the middleware in parallel workers, recording every verdict. Expected supporting result: each request is consistently rejected or accepted according to the state read, with no panic. Falsifier: a request succeeds after disablement or the fixture crashes. Cleanup: stop workers and restore the final flag. Limitation: this tests the fixture store rather than a distributed settings cache.

Hypothesis: the saved patch is robust to minor line-ending variation when applied by common patch tooling. Prerequisites: two pristine copies of the same source, one with LF and one with CRLF line endings, and the saved hunk. Bounded test: apply the patch to both copies, compare the resulting source bytes, and verify the same disabled-token result where the harness can run. Expected supporting result: both applications succeed and produce equivalent source semantics. Falsifier: one copy rejects the hunk or produces different code. Cleanup: delete both copies. Limitation: the official host applies the patch to a Linux snapshot, so this is a packaging robustness check.

evaluations.rationale: The incumbent pristine-tree portability result is established and needs no repetition. It is deferred because it cannot answer the remaining middleware fail-open question.

Selected. It turns the parser-level rejection into a server-boundary question: does the middleware return unauthenticated or treat the disabled result as anonymous? The disabled rejection is already observed, so this adds the downstream propagation evidence needed for the handoff.
Deferred and folded into the selected server check as the positive control. An enabled token must still put its subject into the handler context, proving the middleware is not over-blocking.
Deferred, not refuted. Project-role independence is already established at parser level; a middleware role control is useful but secondary to the disabled-account propagation question.

Deferred, not refuted. A concurrent toggle race needs a mutable settings store and many iterations. The predicate reads an account copy from an informer-backed store, so the simpler propagation test is higher value.

Deferred, not refuted. Line-ending portability is a real packaging concern, but the host applies the patch to a Linux source snapshot and the hunk context is small. It is less informative than the server-boundary check.

observation.summary: Ran a server-package test on the pristine patched tree. A validly signed token for the disabled account was presented through the gRPC metadata token slot to the authentication middleware. The middleware returned an unauthenticated error carrying the parser's disabled-account message, so it did not fall back to an anonymous identity. A valid enabled account token in the same middleware returned no error and placed subject A in the handler context, proving the rejection did not over-block enabled sessions. Project-role middleware behavior was not exercised in this server fixture. Local only; no official evaluation ran.
observation.next_hint: The local evidence and patch are complete for the account-token mechanism; the remaining step is the external host-side evaluator, which may still reject the patch or expose an untested behavior.
